title: What It Really Means To Have High Expectations
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that the phrase "high expectations" has become a cliche so overused that most teachers only vaguely grasp what it means. He contends that high expectations are not techniques you deploy but a quality of character, born of a lifetime of overcoming obstacles, that must genuinely live inside the teacher. That inner conviction, he writes, is not something a poster or a principal can hand a teacher; it has to be developed personally. Students sense this quality even when it goes unspoken, and it is what makes them believe a teacher's declarations about their potential are true. He connects this inner force to why some teachers can give a single direction and have it followed instantly, while others struggle despite using the same words. The piece closes by describing how a teacher's authentic, unshakeable belief transfers into students, giving them their own gutsy, never-say-die spirit.
points: High expectations are not a technique or a phrase to repeat, but an internal quality of character built through the teacher's own life experience.
Talk about high expectations is cheap; what matters is the invisible force of will that students can feel even when it isn't spoken aloud.
Students believe a teacher's stated belief in them ("You can do this") because they sense the authenticity behind it.
This inner conviction explains why certain teachers can give one direction to a brand-new class and have it instantly followed.
A teacher's genuine high expectations become internalized by students, giving them their own resilient, determined spirit.
quotes: It seems obvious, but the term has been repeated so often and for so long that its true meaning has been diluted.
They don’t come from a motivational poster . Your principal doesn’t bequeath them to you. And you darn sure won’t find them in a teacher’s guide.

They come from inside you. They’re developed over a lifetime of overcoming obstacles and disappointments. They’re born of perseverance, mental toughness, and the role models who passed them on to you.
This is why certain teachers can give a direction one time to a class they’ve just met and it’s followed. This is why some classes make unimaginable gains and unheard of test scores.
High expectations that come from within you, that relentlessly project their power upon your students, become part of them too. They imbue them with their own brand of gutsy, I’ll-show-them spirit.
